newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav arms factory ends six weeks of protests.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav arms factory ends six weeks of protests.

text.p: The independent union at Zastava Arms, Yugoslavia's biggest weapons manufacturer, on Thursday called off a series of rolling protests that have continued for the past six weeks.
"We decided to suspend protests until October 22nd, when we will inform workers about our talks with management," the union president Zoran Nedeljkovic told Reuters.

Thousands of Zastava's workers held their hour-long protests in the main square of Kragujevac since August 19, demanding unpaid wages and holiday pay, a programme to revive production and the sacking of top company managers.
Since then, the company's general manager, his deputy, commercial and sales managers have resigned, and wages for June, July and part of August, as well as holiday pay, have been paid.
"Our basic demands have now been met and the trade union has agreed to hold talks with the management," said Nedeljkovic.
"Whether we will reach some agreement by October 22 or have to continue our protests will depend on the outcome of those talks," he added.
Sanctions severed the factory from its foreign contracts and the break-up of the former Yugoslavia shrank its domestic market, leaving it with virtually no buyers.
Nedeljkovic did not wish to comment on statements by government officials that unproductive factories such as Zastava Arms would have to cut down on surplus labour.

"We do expect the number of workers to be reduced compared to the first half of the year, but now that sanctions have been lifted, we also expect the reactivation of certain contracts with foreign partners."
Serbian Finance Minister Dusan Vlatkovic recently said there was no justification to provide credits to Zastava Arms.
"We will never produce or export as much arms as we did in the former Yugoslavia," he said, adding it would be better to redirect Zastava Arm's workers into "production that has a market."
Zastava Arms has concluded a deal worth 9.74 million dinars with the Yugoslav Army, but trade union officials said this would not be enough to ensure the plant's recovery.
The state news agency Tanjug quoted acting general manager Branko Smigic as warning it would be difficult to make up for what was lost over the past one-and-a-half months.

"Several tens of thousands of hours are lost, so it is hard to say whether all production plans for this year can be achieved," Tanjug quoted Smigic as saying. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
